STYLE: HAND-DRAWN INK AND WASH (for informal, thinking-aloud lessons; reflection; a sketchbook voice)
- A skilled illustrator's location sketch: perspective drawn by eye but sound, line drives the drawing, with real variation in weight and a slight natural wobble (no ruler-perfect lines, no shaky jitter either).
- Ink in lm-outline: the near objects in a 3 to 4 px line, the far wall in 1.5 px; lines overshoot slightly at corners; some edges are left open where the light hits.
- Wash in two or three transparent tones per material, laid loosely and not filling to the line everywhere; the paper (wall or paper colour) is left untouched where the light is strongest.
- Hatching or a darker wash only in the shadow side and under things.
- Work outside-in: the big silhouettes and the few large dark shapes first, detail last; one decisive line, not five; heavier lines on near objects, overlaps and the undersides of forms; the wash never repeats what the ink already says.
- Light: Light is the paper left white; shadow is a cool wash in the shadow colour at 0.2 to 0.3 opacity, with hatching in the deepest places.
- Texture: Paper fibres as sparse fine vector strokes in lm-texture; wash edges a little irregular (blooms) on 2 or 3 large areas.
- Depth: Far: thin line, almost no wash. Mid: line and wash. Near: the strongest line and the darkest wash.
- Quality bar: A page from a professional illustrator's sketchbook of a real office: loose, confident, specific.

THE WORLD: TRAVEL AND HOSPITALITY
A mid-sized international airport on the flat edge of a temperate coastal city, and the places a trip passes through around it, all built between 2014 and 2018 to one architect's design: the terminal (a 220 m long check-in hall and a pier of eight gates under one long roof of pale timber), a narrow-body jet at a gate, a 160-room hotel across the forecourt, and the contact centre of a mid-sized travel company on the second floor of an office building in the airport's business park, its windows looking out over the airfield.
Architecture:
- the terminal roof: long-span glued-laminated timber beams of pale spruce at 7.2 m centres with a slatted pale timber soffit between them, carried on slim white steel columns that branch into four arms just under the roof; the check-in hall is about 9 m high at its eaves and 12 m at its ridge, the gate pier about 5 m
- full-height glass walls in tall panes 1.5 m wide between slim white aluminium mullions, with a transom at about 3 m; the panes above the transom carry a fine frit of small white dots that softens the sun
- floors of pale grey terrazzo with fine white and dark chips, laid in large bays with thin brass divider strips, and a charcoal terrazzo band along the main walking routes
- fittings in pale oak and white powder-coated steel; feature panels in deep teal, the airport's colour: the backs of the check-in islands, the gate walls, the hotel's desk wall

- the hotel and the business-park office repeat the terminal's language at room scale: pale timber slat ceilings, terrazzo or oak floors, white steel, deep teal felt and upholstery, and big windows toward the airport
- the aircraft is a twin-engine narrow-body jet with one aisle and six seats abreast; inside, off-white wall and ceiling panels and grey-blue bins, seats in deep teal fabric with pale grey headrest covers; outside, plain white with a pale grey belly, no livery, no logo, no letters

THE SET TO DRAW: departure_gate: a departure gate on the terminal's pier: a two-position gate podium in front of a deep teal gate wall, beam seating in the foreground, and the full-height airside glass on the left with the jet bridge door and a plain white jet's nose at the bridge, under a slatted pale timber ceiling (shots it serves: wide, mid; used for disruption and cancellations at the gate, rebooking and passenger care, overbooking, boarding and document checks, waiting passengers and duty of care)

========== SET 3 of 3 ==========
THE SET TO DRAW: aircraft_cabin: the economy cabin of the plain white narrow-body jet seen from the forward entry area down its single aisle: rows of deep teal seats three and three, grey-blue overhead bins, small windows with their shades part down, and a plain rear bulkhead with a pale grey curtain at the far end (shots it serves: mid, wide; used for cabin crew and passengers: a disruptive or anxious passenger, a medical event, assistance on board, safety and exit rows, delays on the ground)

The cabin is about 3.7 m wide at shoulder height and 2.2 m high at the aisle.
- Seats: six abreast in two blocks of three, each seat 0.46 m wide between armrests 0.05 m wide, seat cushion 0.43 m high, armrests 0.62 m, seat back top (with its headrest cover) 1.12 m; left block x -1.835 to -0.255, right block x 0.255 to 1.835; the aisle between them 0.51 m wide at armrest height. Rows 0.79 m apart (31 inches): row 1's cushion front at y 0.9, row k's at y 0.9 + 0.79 (k - 1); each seat back stands about 0.5 to 0.6 m behind its cushion front. The seats face forward, toward the camera. Rows 10 and 11 are the overwing exit rows.
- Side walls: off-white lining panels curving in toward the bins, one small rounded window (0.23 by 0.31 m, centre about 1.1 m up, about a seated passenger's eye level, so its upper half shows over the seat backs) about every 0.53 m, so windows do not line up with the rows; each window has a sliding shade. Above the seats, a passenger service strip (reading lights, air vents, call buttons) runs under the bins at about 1.58 m.
- Overhead bins: grey-blue curved doors with a recessed latch along their lower edge, their lower inner edge about 1.62 m above the floor at x plus or minus 1.0, their tops meeting the off-white ceiling at about 2.05 m; the ceiling over the aisle is 2.2 m high, washed by a hidden light strip along each bin top. - a wide-body cabin with two aisles or a business-class cabin with big seats

- screens in the seat backs or text on any sign (the exit signs are the green running figure with a door and an arrow, no words)
- windows lined up exactly with the rows
- an exit sign, a door frame or a lit lamp right behind the crew member's head at the far end
- a cramped cartoon tube: the cabin is 3.7 m wide and 2.2 m high, with a real person's proportions in it

ORDER
1. Work ONE set at a time. For each: write its short plan (horizon y, vanishing points, focal point, light direction and
   shadow direction, free zones for characters with their anchors, what goes in far, mid and near), draw it, run the
   quality check, fix, save its file. Only then start the next set.
2. Never reuse one set's geometry, camera or furniture layout for another: each follows its own brief.
3. Do not draw any variants until I approve the main sets.

QUALITY CHECK (run it before you reply; redraw what fails and say what you changed)
Layout:
- Layout is cinematography: the camera height, angle and staging are decided before any rendering. Plan every set as far, mid and near ground, and leave clear space for the characters on the floor and around their heads, with breathing room on the side they will face.
- Prefer a low horizon (seated or standing eye height, never a high bird's-eye) so the room is not mostly empty floor and character sizes read clearly.
- Lead the eye with the architecture (a walkway, a table edge, a row of columns, the light pattern) to one focal point; the squint test must still show that focal point and the free space for the characters.
- Keep the backgrounds' values and patterns apart from where characters will stand: no busy pattern or high-contrast edge behind a head.
- Every receding edge goes to its vanishing point; furniture rotated to the room gets its own vanishing points on the same horizon.
- Parallax: draw the walls and floor complete behind the furniture (no holes when layers slide), run the far layer past the frame edges into the overscan, and keep the near layer to one or two framing objects.
- Cast shadows and contact shadows on everything that touches a surface; without them objects look pasted in.
Real-world sense (nothing absurd):
- The horizon is the one in the camera line; furniture sits ON the floor with contact shadows; nothing floats,
  intersects a wall or passes through another object.
- Sizes agree with the scale list: chairs fit under tables, doors are taller than people, screens and windows are
  the stated sizes, steps and sills are reachable.
- The set was drawn, not modelled: soft things have curved edges, chairs have shaped backs and seats, and no shape is
  an unexplained slab or patch.
- Every object reads at a glance and in silhouette as what it is (a chair as a chair, a plant as a real plant);
  every object listed in the scene is present, and nothing is there that would not be in this place.
- Light has one logic: every cast shadow falls away from the named source at a consistent angle; screens and lamps
  glow only if they are on in this version.
- No people, no letters, numbers or logos; slots are empty rects; the palette is exact.
Not in this style:
- uniform, mechanical line weight
- every area washed (no paper left)
- jittery 'hand-drawn filter' wobble
- children's doodle simplification
- a heavy outline on every object, or equal detail everywhere
Not in this world:
- real airlines, airports, hotels, travel brands, logos, liveries, tail colours, registration letters, uniforms of a real company, flags or anything that pins a country
- words, letters or numbers on any sign, screen, board, ticket, tag or display: pictograms and arrows only, and slots where text would be
- people in the sets (the cast is separate)
- a glossy sci-fi terminal (chrome, neon, lens flares) or a grim, dirty one
- a jumbo jet, a propeller plane or a cartoon plane: the aircraft is the same plain white twin-engine narrow-body everywhere
- a red exit sign or one with a word on it: exit signs are green with a running figure, a door and an arrow, and they sit only over real exits
- fire extinguishers standing on the floor, or anything blocking a door, an exit or a gate
- screens in a work area that face a window or stand with a window right behind them
